NT architecture
Which component runs in kernel mode on Windows?
The Windows executive and kernel (ntoskrnl.exe)
The Explorer shell that draws the desktop and taskbar
The Microsoft Edge browser and its rendering engine
The Task Manager application started from the taskbar
ntoskrnl.exe holds the executive and kernel; Explorer, Edge and Task Manager are user-mode programs.
m
Sessions
Why do services on modern Windows run in session 0?
To isolate services from interactive user sessions
To give services a faster path to the graphics card
To let services display windows on every user's desktop
To allow services to start before the kernel is loaded
Session 0 isolation separates services from user desktops, reducing attacks where users interact with privileged service windows.
d
System folders
Why is a program named svchost.exe running from C:\Users\Public suspicious?
The genuine svchost.exe lives in C:\Windows\System32
svchost.exe is only ever started by a logged-in administrator
svchost.exe cannot run on Windows 10 or Windows 11 at all
Files in C:\Users\Public are always deleted at logoff
Masquerading uses legitimate names from unusual paths. Path and parent process are key checks.
d
Process ancestry
Which parent process is normal for services.exe?
wininit.exe
explorer.exe
winword.exe
cmd.exe
wininit.exe starts services.exe, lsass.exe and others. A services.exe with a different parent is a red flag.

Registry root keys
Which registry root key holds machine-wide configuration?
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
HKEY_CURRENT_USER
HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT only
HKEY_USERS\.DEFAULT only
HKLM holds machine settings; HKCU holds the current user's settings.
m
Hives and files
Where is the current user's registry hive stored on disk?
NTUSER.DAT in the user's profile folder
SYSTEM in C:\Windows\System32\config
pagefile.sys at the root of drive C
hiberfil.sys in the user's profile folder
Each user's HKCU is loaded from NTUSER.DAT in their profile; machine hives are in System32\config.
d
Persistence locations
Why do defenders review HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run?
Programs listed there start automatically when the user logs on
It records every program the user has ever uninstalled
It contains the user's password hash in encrypted form
It stores the firewall rules that apply to the user
Run keys are among the most common persistence locations for malware and unwanted software.
m
Value types
Which registry value type stores a 32-bit number?
REG_DWORD
REG_SZ
REG_MULTI_SZ
REG_BINARY
REG_DWORD is a 32-bit integer; REG_SZ is a string and REG_MULTI_SZ a list of strings.
m
Services and the SCM
Where is a Windows service's configuration, such as its binary path, stored?
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Services
C:\Windows\Temp\services.ini
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\Services
Each service has a key under CurrentControlSet\Services with ImagePath, Start type and account.
d
Service permissions
A low-privilege user can modify a service's ImagePath. Why is that a privilege escalation risk?
They can point the service at their own program, which then runs with the service's account
They can read the service's memory and extract the administrator password
They can stop the service, which automatically grants them administrator rights
They can rename the service so that antivirus stops scanning it
Weak service permissions let attackers redirect what a privileged service executes.
m
Service accounts
Which built-in account is a low-privilege option for a service that needs no network identity?
LocalService
LocalSystem
Administrator
krbtgt
LocalService has minimal local rights. LocalSystem has the broadest rights; krbtgt is a domain Kerberos account.
m
SIDs
What is a security identifier (SID)?
A unique value that identifies a user, group or computer
The password hash used to log on to the system
The serial number of the computer's TPM chip
The name of the domain controller that created the account
Windows grants access by SID, not by name. Renaming an account keeps its SID.
d
Well-known RIDs
Why does renaming the built-in Administrator account give only limited protection?
Its SID still ends in the well-known RID 500
Renaming deletes the account's password
Windows ignores renamed accounts at logon
Renamed accounts lose administrator rights
Tools can find the account by its RID 500 regardless of its name.
m
Built-in groups
Which local group grants full control of a Windows computer?
Administrators
Users
Guests
Remote Desktop Users
Members of Administrators can change anything on the machine; Users and Guests are restricted.
d
LAPS
What problem does Windows LAPS solve?
Identical local administrator passwords across many machines
Users forgetting their domain passwords at logon
Slow logons caused by large user profiles
Lost BitLocker keys on removable drives
LAPS sets a unique, rotated local administrator password per device and stores it securely, blocking lateral movement with one shared password.
m
Access tokens
What does a Windows access token describe?
The identity, groups and privileges of a process
The list of files a user opened during the day
The encryption key used for the user's disk
The network address of the user's computer
Every process carries a token. Access checks compare it with the object's security descriptor.
d
UAC split token
Why does an administrator's Explorer process normally run with a filtered token?
UAC removes admin rights until elevation is approved
Explorer cannot run with administrator rights at all
Filtered tokens make the desktop start more quickly
Filtered tokens are required to access the internet
UAC gives admins a standard token by default, so malware launched from their session does not silently get full rights.
d
Privileges
Why is SeDebugPrivilege significant to defenders?
It allows opening other processes, including LSASS, to read their memory
It allows a user to debug only the programs they have written themselves
It is required for any user to start Microsoft Visual Studio
It prevents a process from being terminated by Task Manager
SeDebugPrivilege lets a process access almost any other process. Credential theft tools rely on it.
m
Integrity levels
What does Mandatory Integrity Control prevent?
Lower-integrity processes writing to higher-integrity objects
Users logging on outside their permitted hours
Programs connecting to the internet without consent
Files being copied to USB drives without approval
A low-integrity process (such as a sandboxed browser tab) cannot modify medium- or high-integrity objects.
d
LSASS protection
What does running LSASS as a protected process (RunAsPPL) aim to stop?
Non-protected processes reading its memory for credentials
LSASS being started by the Windows kernel at boot
Users changing their own passwords at logon
Domain controllers replicating password changes
PPL blocks ordinary processes, even admin ones, from opening LSASS memory, which hinders credential dumping.
m
NTFS permissions
Which NTFS permission lets a user change file contents but not change permissions or take ownership?
Modify
Full Control
Read and Execute
List Folder Contents
Modify includes write and delete; only Full Control adds changing permissions and taking ownership.
d
ACE evaluation
A user is in one group allowed Read and another group explicitly denied Read on a file. What happens?
Access is denied, because explicit deny takes precedence
Access is allowed, because allow entries are checked first
Windows asks the user which group to use at access time
The result depends on which group was created most recently
Explicit deny ACEs are ordered first and override allows at the same level.
m
Inheritance
What does permission inheritance mean in NTFS?
Child files and folders take permissions from their parent
Files keep the permissions of the user who deleted them
Permissions copy from one drive letter to every other drive
New users automatically receive the permissions of their manager
Inherited ACEs flow from parent folders, which keeps large trees consistent.
d
Share versus NTFS
A share grants Everyone Full Control and NTFS grants a user Read. What can the user do over the network?
Read only, because the more restrictive of the two applies
Full Control, because share permissions override NTFS
Nothing, because Everyone entries are ignored
Write only, because the two permissions are combined
Over the network, the effective access is the most restrictive of share and NTFS permissions.
m
Viewing permissions
Which command-line tool displays and edits NTFS permissions?
icacls
chmod
ipconfig
netstat
icacls shows and changes ACLs on Windows; chmod is the Linux equivalent concept.
d
Least privilege on NTFS
Why should permissions be granted to groups rather than to individual users?
Group membership changes are easier to manage and audit
Windows cannot apply permissions to individual users
Individual permissions slow down every file access
Groups encrypt the files they are given access to
Role-based groups make joiners, movers and leavers simple and keep ACLs readable.
